rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · Beth Finds the Palace Beautiful
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a small shy girl with braided hair sitting at a grand piano in a stately parlor while a tall old gentleman with silver hair listens from a wing chair, sunlight through tall lace curtains, a framed portrait on the wall, gentle warm light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The little piano from next door stood in the March parlor, and Beth played it every day. Her fingers grew braver, and the tunes came out clear and sweet. But one hard thing was still left to do. She must go and thank old Mr. Laurence with her own lips. To Beth, the grand house next door was a palace. The stern old man who owned it seemed more fearful than any giant in her storybooks. Laurie begged her to come. “Grandfather asks about you every single day,” he said. But Beth always shook her head and hid behind her sewing.
Beth slips through the garden gate to thank the old gentleman for the piano.

One golden afternoon she made up her mind. She slipped through the little gate between the two gardens, quiet as a mouse. The mansion was cool and still as a church. In the drawing room stood the splendid grand piano, shining like a lake. Beth forgot her fear and touched the keys. Music rose like a bird let out of a cage. She played on and on with her eyes shut. She never heard the door open softly behind her. She never saw the old gentleman come in and stand there listening.
Talk together: Beth feared one kind old man all year. What small brave thing could you do this week, even if it shakes you?

Beth sprang up, white with fright. But Mr. Laurence spoke as gently as a grandfather should. He showed her a little picture of a girl he had loved and lost long ago. Then he told Beth she might come and play any day she liked. “The piano and the room are yours,” he said. Beth found her voice at last and whispered her thank you. After that she came often. She made the old man warm slippers with her own hands, and he wore them proudly. The palace next door kept one door always open for her.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · Being Neighborly
chapters.artPrompt: a girl in a plain green dress laughing in a handsome library beside a boy lying on a sofa with a red nose and a blanket, a cat on his knee, tall bookshelves and a portrait on the wall, warm afternoon light through heavy curtains, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Just as the two houses were growing close, Laurie caught a terrible cold. He lay on the sofa in the great mansion with a red nose and nothing to do but sneeze. When Jo heard of it she marched straight over. Her arms were full of apples, her cat, and two of her funniest books. “A sick boy all alone is a shame and a waste,” she said. “I have come to make you laugh whether you like it or not.” And soon Laurie was laughing till he coughed, which is the best medicine in the world.
Jo brings her cat and her funniest books to cheer a sneezing Laurie.

Between laughs Laurie showed her the house. They wandered through cool halls and into the library, where a thousand books stood in shelves to the ceiling. Jo gasped like a sailor seeing land. They talked too about the master of the house. “Grandfather is proud and lonely,” said Laurie. “He has lost a great deal, and he never speaks of it.” Jo nodded slowly. “Then we must make this old house jollier,” she said. “Lonely rooms are bad for sick boys and old men too.” So she promised to come again, and she always kept her promises.
New word: mansion — a very large, grand house. Laurie has the mansion; Jo has the noise and the fun.

On the stairs they met old Mr. Laurence himself, tall and silver and stern. Jo looked straight at him and saw Laurie grown old. She spoke her honest mind without stopping to be afraid. “You are proud, sir, but you are not hard,” she said. “And your boy is the finest boy in town.” The old gentleman’s stern face broke into a smile. He told her she might come whenever she pleased, and he meant it. That evening the mansion felt warm for the first time in years. From that day the two gardens were hardly two gardens at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Week of Rest
chapters.artPrompt: four girls in crumpled aprons and untidy hair sitting around a kitchen table with a ruined supper of hard peas and burnt bread, a bird cage with a drooping canary on the window sill, late afternoon light, funny and gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: By and by all four sisters were tired of work. Meg sewed for other people all day. Jo ran errands for cross old Aunt March. Beth scrubbed and cooked, and Amy went to school with a sore head over her sums. “Let us play for one whole week,” said Meg, “like rich people, with nothing to do.” Mother smiled a strange little smile, and said they might try. So duty was sent packing for seven days. Nobody washed a dish, and nobody felt guilty — at first.
The great picnic supper fails: hard peas, sour bread, and no salt at all.

The first days were heavenly. Jo read novels in a heap of cushions until her head ached. Meg trifled away the hours with gossip and ribbons. Amy sketched whatever she saw, and drew it badly. Only Beth went quietly on with her work, for somebody must mind the canary and the cat. Then came the great day when the girls cooked a grand picnic dinner. The peas were hard as marbles. The bread was sour. The salt stood forgotten on the shelf, and the pudding was a sad wet hill. Meg burned her finger, Jo upset the coffee, and Amy tasted everything twice.
Talk together: the girls wanted a holiday, and got one. Why did work begin to look sweet again by Saturday?

Worst of all, poor Kitty the canary drooped and died for want of care. The girls were very sorry indeed. By the end of the week they crept back to their duties like tired travelers coming home. Funny enough, work felt pleasant again. Even the scrubbing bucket looked friendly, and the needles flew merrily. Mother never said one word of lecture. She only laughed quietly in her room. The girls remembered the week of rest all their lives. They remembered its lesson too: all play and no work makes even play grow stale.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · Meg Goes to Vanity Fair
chapters.artPrompt: a young girl in a borrowed blue silk gown with piled curls standing uneasy among fashionably dressed girls before a ballroom mirror, candlelight and bouquets, a boy in a neat suit watching sadly from the doorway, soft warm light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Then Meg was invited to spend two whole weeks with the rich Moffat family. There were fine sisters there, and finer gowns. On the last evening the Moffat girls dressed Meg up in borrowed blue silk. They piled her hair in curls, hung jewels at her throat, and laced her so tight she could hardly breathe. Meg looked in the glass and hardly knew the fine lady there. She was pleased, and yet her heart felt strangely heavy all the evening. She laughed and danced, and wished she did not feel like a doll.
Laurie finds Meg in borrowed silk, and wishes for the Meg he knows.

At the party someone poured sweet wine into her glass. Meg, not wishing to seem a baby, drank it. Soon her cheeks burned and her head swam. Just then Laurie came, and his face fell when he saw her. “That is not you,” he said sadly. “I like you best in your own plain muslin.” The words stung Meg worse than any scolding. She went home the next day feeling small and confused. She was very glad to see her own dear home again. And the borrowed splendor began to itch before it was off.
New word: vanity — caring too much for fine looks and what people think of them. It never fills the heart.

Mother listened to the whole story with kind eyes. “I want my girls to be beautiful, useful, and happy,” she said, “but not to be fine ladies. I would rather see you poor and beloved than rich and false.” Meg cried a little, and was comforted. She folded the borrowed dream away. She put on her old apron, and found her own life sweeter than any mirror at the Moffats’. And she quietly told Laurie, the next time they met, that he had done her more good than he knew. Meg kept her word, and the plain muslin never once felt poor again.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · A Whisper of Gossip
chapters.artPrompt: two girls whispering behind hands on a snowy school fence while another girl in a plain coat walks past with her chin up, town rooftops and bare trees, cold morning light, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: One winter day Laurie came over red-faced and angry. The schoolboys had been joking that Meg was going to marry rich Laurie. They laughed as if she would take his fine house and be a grand lady. Jo’s eyes blazed like fire. She wanted to shake every boy in town and set the whole school straight. Meg only turned pink and said nothing. But her needles went very fast, and nobody dared to ask why. The teapot nearly boiled over while she sat there burning.
Meg says little while the needles fly, and Jo plans a thunderstorm.

“Let them talk,” said Mother at supper. “Idle talk dies of hunger when nobody feeds it. If Meg goes calmly on, the joke will starve.” But Jo grumbled all evening, and Meg lay awake whispering with her sister in the dark. “I would not mind the tattling,” Meg said at last. “But I do mind the world thinking a girl must always be hunting for a rich husband.” “Then let us show them another way to live,” said Jo fiercely. Meg felt better for saying it. And Jo felt braver for hearing it.
Question for you: someone repeats a joke about you that is not true. What is stronger — an angry answer, or a calm one?

The whisper ran round the town for a week or two, as whispers do. Then it found no more to eat, and it died. The sisters kept their plan: to work, to love each other, and to let fools talk. But Jo watched Meg after that, whenever a quiet young man came near. She kept one fist closed inside her mitten, ready for trouble. And the winter went by, busy and bright, with more work in it than ever and more fun than work. Even Laurie was careful after that, for he had learned what teasing costs. And Meg, walking to her sewing each morning, held her head a little higher than before.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Pickwick Portfolio
chapters.artPrompt: children in 1860s clothes gathered by candlelight in a dusty attic around a small table covered with handwritten pages, one girl with a paper reading aloud while others laugh, an old stove and hanging herbs, warm golden lamplight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Up in the attic, behind the old costumes and boxes, the March sisters kept a secret club. Every member took a grand funny name out of a beloved old book, and Jo was the editor. Once a week the club printed its own paper, called the Pickwick Portfolio. It held stories, news, riddles, and advertisements, all written out in Jo’s best hand. “Every member must bring something,” Jo declared. “Or pay a penny fine, hot from the purse.” The penalty was never questioned, for the court was fierce and the purse was small. The attic was the club’s castle, and the Portfolio was its flag.
The club gathers by candlelight while the editor reads the week’s paper aloud.

The papers were read aloud on club nights, and the attic shook with laughter. Amy wrote advertisements with grand misspelled words. One of them offered a lost kite, with a reward of one whole cent. Meg sent in the fashion news. Beth kept the quiet little notes of kindness. Even Laurie begged to join, and the sisters voted him in after long argument. He paid his fine in roasted peanuts, which the club ate before the meeting ended. And his jokes, Jo had to admit, were good enough for any editor in the land.
Talk together: the club makes its own fun with paper and candlelight. What could your family or friends make together this month?

There was only one law of the club: no unkind word might ever be printed in the Portfolio. The paper grew thicker every week, and the club grew prouder of it. Nobody became rich or famous, and nobody wanted to. The old attic, smelling of dust and apples, held a treasure that fine houses could not buy. It held a family laughing over its own bright, silly, precious pages. And whenever money was scarce and tempers short, one club night could put the whole house right again. That was the kind of wealth the club understood best.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · The Post Office in the Hedge
chapters.artPrompt: an old wooden birdhouse nailed to a garden fence post with a little slit door, a girl in a green dress posting a letter while a boy hurries up the snowy path from a mansion beyond the hedge, winter afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Between the March garden and the Laurence garden stood a hedge. On a fence post of that hedge somebody nailed an old wooden birdhouse. It had a little slit door and a hook for letters. Laurie painted the words POST OFFICE over it in grand letters. From that day the two houses could send secrets without crossing the snow. Notes flew back and forth all day long, like small white birds. The maids laughed at it at first, and then began to use it too. And Beth was the first to trust it with a real secret.
Every kind of letter drops through the little slit, silly or sad or glad.

The letters were of every kind. Laurie sent verses that did not always rhyme. Jo sent jokes and challenges. Meg sent pretty notes. Beth, who feared the big house, sent a brave little thank-you of her own. One cold evening the sisters found a letter in a fine old hand. It was from Mr. Laurence himself. He asked to be made a member of all their fun, and promised to pay his postage in kindness. The club voted him in with three cheers.
New word: hedge — a row of bushes planted as a living fence. Two gardens, one hedge, one little door for friendship.

No letter was ever too small for the post office, and none was ever laughed at but in love. Now and then a grumbling sister found a sudden joke waiting on the hook, and grumbles melted like snow. The hedge between two gardens had found a door. Through that little slit went more riches than the great mansion next door ever held. And if you had asked any of the children of the two houses, they would all have agreed. The post office was the best thing in town. Beth’s first real secret was about the old man’s cat, and it stayed safe for years.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · Camp Laurence
chapters.artPrompt: a June picnic by a shining river among tall trees, young people in 1860s summer clothes playing croquet on the grass, a white tent, a girl in a light dress handing pickled limes from a small box, sailboats far out on the water, bright warm noon, storybook illustration

blocks.text: In June Laurie gave a grand picnic in the woods by the river, at a camp he called Camp Laurence. The guests came in wagons: the Moffat girls, an English cousin named Kate, and quiet Mr. Brooke, who was Laurie’s tutor. The day was as bright as a new coin. Croquet hoops went up on the grass. Boats waited on the water. And a small box of pickled limes went round and round like a kindly little sun. Even the wagon ride out was part of the fun, packed in among hampers and hats.
Games on the grass and limes for everyone, while a quiet tutor watches Meg.

The English cousin looked down her nose at American games. Jo’s temper rose like bread dough, until the girls made peace over a shared boat. There were races in the woods and races on the river. Supper came out of baskets under the trees, and everybody ate twice as much as at home. It was the kind of day that smells of hay and water. It would stay golden in the memory for years. Even Kate forgot to be grand, and laughed till her rings rattled.
Talk together: the picnic mixed grand manners and plain ones. When did laughter make everyone equal that day?

At packing-up time Meg dropped one white glove on the grass and never missed it. Nobody saw. Nobody — except Jo, who happened to look back. She saw quiet Mr. Brooke pick up the little glove and slip it into his breast pocket, softly as a thief. Jo said nothing at all. But a small cloud crossed her sunny day. She carried it home with the empty baskets, wondering what it could mean. Meg hummed all the way home, and did not know that anything in the world had changed. Gloves are small things. But some small things change whole lives.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 · Castles in the Air
chapters.artPrompt: four sisters in 1860s dresses and a boy in a summer suit sitting in a circle on a brown autumn hillside among goldenrod and purple asters, pointing at a far bright cloud in a blue sky, roofs of a small town below, soft afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: One September afternoon the four sisters and Laurie climbed the brown hill behind the town. Goldenrod burned yellow there, and asters stood purple among the stubble. The air smelled of dry grass and late summer. The town lay small and quiet below. They lay in the dry grass, and somebody began the old game called castles in the air. Each one must tell the dream house they would live in someday, if wishes were deeds. The clouds sailed slowly over, and the castles rose. It was the pleasantest game in the world, and it cost nothing.
Dreams stand up like castles while the clouds sail over the hill.

Meg’s castle held a kind husband, rosy children, and a house full of comfort. Amy’s stood in Rome, with marble studios and the finest statues in the world. Beth’s castle was only the old gray house, with all of them in it, safe and together. Nobody laughed at all, because it was the best castle of the four. Jo’s had fine horses and a magic inkstand that never ran dry. It had her name in bright letters on a hundred books. Dreams were going up like smoke, and nobody wanted to stop them.
Question for you: if wishes were deeds, what would your castle in the air look like? Draw it or say it aloud.

Laurie said his castle was the whole world. He would travel and see everything, then come home rich in wonder and do good with his money. “Some day we will climb this hill again,” he said, “and count which dreams came true.” The sun went down behind the little town. They came down the hill slowly, still talking, still half in their castles. Each one secretly believed that hers, at least, would come true. And the wind over the hill kept their secrets till they came again. Laurie carried a basket of apples, and the apples got eaten before the top of the hill.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 · Jo's Story Sold
chapters.artPrompt: a girl with wavy hair waving a letter above her head in a small parlor while three sisters and a mother in a gray dress crowd around laughing, sheet music and sewing on the table, firelight on the walls, joyful warm evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Every night when the house was quiet, Jo climbed to the garret with her ink and paper. She wrote stories — stirring tales, with storms and shipwrecks and bold heroes. She loved every wild word of them. One day she wrapped her best story, sent it to a newspaper, and waited. Weeks went by. She waited more, and scolded herself for a goose, and waited still. The garret spiders grew used to her pacing, and went on with their own spinning.
The letter is opened, and one hundred dollars leaps out of a plain envelope.

Then a fat envelope came, and the house heard Jo scream. The story would be printed — and there was a check for one hundred dollars inside. Jo waved it round the parlor like a flag of victory. She bought presents with her prize. New sheet music for Beth, pretty ribbons for Meg and Amy, and a warm shawl for Mother. Then she sat down feeling ten feet tall, and much too grand for the little house. But that feeling did not last past supper.
Talk together: Jo earned money doing the thing she loved. What would you buy first if your own work paid you one day?

“Take care, my Jo,” Mother said, smiling. “Money and praise are sweet, but they can spoil a writer faster than failure. Write what is true and good, and the rest will follow or not, as it pleases.” Jo promised, though her eyes still shone. The family read the story aloud on Sunday. Jo hid under a cushion through all the exciting parts. That night the garret lamp burned late. And the garret spiders, going on with their spinning, kept the secret of the famous author upstairs. Jo read the printed story at breakfast, and the family listened with their spoons in the air. It sounded even better in print, she thought, though she said so only to Beth.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 · The Secret
chapters.artPrompt: a boy in a smart suit whispering earnestly to a girl in a plain green dress on a garden wall in winter, the girl's face frowning with worry, bare apple trees and a grand house beyond, cold bright afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Laurie came whistling over the snow one afternoon, then stopped whistling and fidgeted instead. He had a secret, and it burned in him like a coin in the pocket. Jo guessed it was something large, for Laurie only fidgeted over big things. “Spit it out,” she said. So he leaned close and whispered his news. Jo’s face went from pink to red to a stormy gray. The snow kept falling softly, and did not care what it was falling on.
Laurie whispers, and Jo hears that her safe world is about to tilt.

The news was this: Mr. Brooke, the quiet tutor, kept Meg’s lost glove and carried it near his heart. He spoke of Meg tenderly, and meant to ask her to marry him before long. “I hate it!” cried Jo, marching up and down the room. “Meg is too young! We are not ready! I won’t have it!” Laurie warned her that lovers do not wait upon sisters. But Jo would not hear a word. She declared she would send Meg away to Aunt March for ten years.
New word: tender — gentle and loving, the way one holds something precious. Mr. Brooke spoke of Meg tenderly.

Jo went home with her head high and her heart heavy as lead. Meg sat by the window, singing softly over her sewing, sweet and completely unaware. Jo looked at her a long time, and something in her ached. “Nobody shall hurry her,” she said to herself. “Not the tutor, not the world, not anybody.” She kept watch that evening like a little soldier. She did not sleep well. Meg never once looked up. Perhaps that was the saddest part of all. That night Jo wrote in her journal that she would guard Meg with her life. Then she blew out the candle, and lay in the dark listening to the snow. She thought of Mr. Brooke’s quiet face.
